question.worked_solution:
Let $u=2x+1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that $x=\frac{1}{2}(u-1).$ 

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $-1/2$ | $3/2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $0$ | $4$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/2}^{3/2}4x\sqrt{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{4}4\cdot \frac{1}{2}(u-1)\cdot \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}({u}^{3/2}-{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & ={(\frac{1}{(5/2)}{u}^{5/2}-\frac{1}{(3/2)}{u}^{3/2})|}_{0}^{4} \\  & ={(\frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2})|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =(\frac{2}{5}\cdot {4}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {4}^{3/2})-(\frac{2}{5}\cdot {0}^{5/2}-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {0}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{64}{5}-\frac{16}{3} \\  & =\frac{112}{15}\end{aligned}
$$
